name: Hosni Mubarak
summary: Mubarak governed Egypt under a continuously renewed state of emergency and sought constitutional changes expanding presidential discretion over security cases and restricting electoral competition. His presidency moved toward private investment and asset sales, while retaining public subsidies. He maintained peace with Israel and sent Egyptian forces to join the coalition that drove Iraq out of Kuwait.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Mubarak’s Article 179 amendment authorized counterterrorism procedures that could override constitutional protection of private communications.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Mubarak kept Egypt under emergency rule throughout his presidency and secured constitutional authority to waive ordinary safeguards in terrorism cases.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Mubarak referred detained Muslim Brotherhood leaders and other members to military trial after a civilian court rejected the charges. His constitutional changes sharply restricted opposition candidacies.

separated-powers.rationale: Mubarak’s 2007 amendment to Article 179 allowed the president to choose the judicial body for terrorism cases. He had already bypassed ordinary courts by referring civilian cases to military tribunals.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Mubarak used broad emergency powers and military courts under provisions of the existing legal framework. The sources do not settle his position on whether rulers should govern only under promulgated laws.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Mubarak’s amendment to Article 5 prohibited political activity or parties organized on a religious basis.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Mubarak initiated the 2005 amendment replacing a yes-or-no referendum on a single nominee with a direct multicandidate presidential vote. His 2007 changes kept direct election while tightly restricting entry.

elective-rulers.rationale: Mubarak introduced a direct election to choose the president from multiple candidates under Article 76, with restrictive nomination conditions.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Mubarak governed for nearly five six-year terms and retained Article 77’s unlimited eligibility for successive terms when he revised the rules for presidential elections.

democracy-best.rationale: Mubarak secured restrictions on competitive candidacies and reduced judicial supervision of elections while seeking to keep the presidency and legislature in his party’s hands.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Mubarak remained head of the National Democratic Party while using presidential powers to rewrite the rules under which it competed for office.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Mubarak’s 2005 decree gave provincial governors the power to approve church expansion and reconstruction. Presidential authorization still governed construction of new churches.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Mubarak revived Egypt’s nuclear power plans and selected Dabaa as the site for its first nuclear generating station.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The record establishes Mubarak’s support for the Dabaa plant. The other material reviewed does not settle whether he wanted the state to direct investment toward strategic industries generally.

public-ownership.rationale: Mubarak’s later presidency sustained privatization across sectors, including banks and telecommunications. In the first nine months of fiscal year 2005–06, the state sold 49 assets, including a stake in Egypt Telecom.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The 2005 reform reduced the top income tax rate while retaining progressive brackets. The sources do not establish where Mubarak stood on how much larger the share paid by wealthy taxpayers should be.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The environmental law in force under Mubarak imposed pollution standards and reporting obligations on covered establishments, with inspections and enforcement by the environmental agency.

strong-leader.rationale: His constitutional reforms expanded executive discretion, but the sources did not directly establish his position on overriding political gridlock.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Construction of the Grand Egyptian Museum began under Mubarak as a large public project to house and display Egyptian antiquities. The Egypt–Sudan charter he signed also identified preservation of inherited traditions as a goal for education.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Mubarak asked the UN to overcome restraints on its ability to respond to states that flouted its resolutions. He cited South Africa’s defiance of Security Council resolutions as an example.

nation-first.rationale: In his 1983 UN address, Mubarak put multilateral cooperation ahead of seeking narrow national advantage at other countries’ expense in responding to shared economic crises.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Mubarak issued a banking law that preserved a public central bank with statutory power to issue currency and regulate banks.

separate-church-state.rationale: Mubarak issued Decree 291 of 2005 giving government officials authority to approve church expansion or reconstruction, and retained presidential authorization for new churches.

civilizational-union.rationale: Mubarak signed the Nile Valley Integration Charter with Sudan, citing the countries’ historical and cultural ties and creating a joint council and parliament.

limit-population.rationale: Mubarak launched a national family-planning campaign in 2008 to slow population growth and encouraged families to have fewer children.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: In his 1983 UN address, Mubarak condemned apartheid South Africa’s racial minority rule and called for implementation of UN resolutions against the regime’s practices.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The 2003 Labour Code enacted during Mubarak’s presidency limited lawful strikes to union procedures and prohibited them in specified vital establishments.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Mubarak agreed with Sudan to share decision-making through an integration council and Nile Valley parliament, with joint bodies charged with planning a staged economic union.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Mubarak personally directed military policy in the Gulf crisis, including deciding on access to Egyptian military bases. The Egyptian force subsequently deployed and fought in Kuwait under his presidency.

death-penalty.rationale: Mubarak personally ratified six death sentences in June 1993 after a military tribunal convicted defendants in a case involving a militant Islamist group.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Mubarak’s 2004 nationality law granted citizenship at birth through an Egyptian father or mother and provided an exception for children found in Egypt whose parents were unknown.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: At the UN in 1983, Mubarak asked developed countries to commit 0.7 percent of national product to development assistance and raise the commitment to 1 percent by 1990.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: At the UN in 1983, Mubarak backed a nuclear-weapon-free Middle East as part of a worldwide nonproliferation and disarmament effort.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Article 5 of the banking law Mubarak issued in 2003 required the central bank to agree its monetary policy objectives with the government through a council established by presidential decree.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Mubarak helped organize the international response to Iraq’s seizure of Kuwait and sent Egyptian forces to reverse the annexation and restore Kuwait’s government.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The 2005 reform reduced the highest personal income rate to 20 percent and left a graduated schedule in place.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Egypt’s personal-status reform under Mubarak allowed women to obtain khul without proving injury or fault if they returned the dowry and waived specified financial rights.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Mubarak’s 2007 amendment to Article 115 required the People’s Assembly to approve the budget by law, title by title, and gave it the power to amend proposed expenditures within specified limits.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: The associations law enacted under Mubarak required domestic NGOs to obtain government permission to accept funding from abroad.

social-market-economy.rationale: Mubarak’s presidency pursued a larger role for private firms while retaining state food subsidies. During the 2008 bread shortage he personally ordered military and Interior Ministry bakeries to increase affordable supplies.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: At the UN in 1983, Mubarak endorsed a nuclear-weapon-free zone in the Middle East that would include Egypt.

second-chamber.rationale: Mubarak’s 2007 amendment to Article 194 gave the Shura Council a formal approval role in specified laws and treaties alongside the People’s Assembly.

arms-reduction.rationale: Mubarak urged global general and complete disarmament and argued that the accumulation of conventional arms itself endangered smaller countries.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: At the UN in 1989, Mubarak called for a change in the international economic arrangements that disadvantaged developing countries through trade barriers, deteriorating terms of trade and rising debt burdens.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Mubarak created the National Council for Women by presidential decree in 2000 to monitor laws and policies affecting women and promote their participation.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Mubarak’s presidency enacted the khul procedure, under which a woman could obtain a divorce without her husband’s consent by relinquishing specified financial claims.

no-central-bank.rationale: Mubarak’s 2003 banking law retained the Central Bank of Egypt as a public body and charged it with conducting monetary, credit and banking policy.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: The amendment Mubarak proposed to Article 136 gave the president power to dissolve the People’s Assembly without first winning a referendum.

mandatory-environmental-reporting.rationale: Egypt’s 2009 environmental amendment required covered businesses to submit impact assessments for proposed projects and maintain environmental records for agency inspections.

reserved-seats-excluded-groups.rationale: Mubarak’s amendment to Article 62 authorized minimum representation of women in elected councils, and the 2009 electoral law subsequently reserved 64 People’s Assembly seats for women.

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: Mubarak issued Law 154 of 2004, which recognized that children who acquired Egyptian nationality through the amended provisions could retain it alongside a foreign nationality.

conquest-no-lawful-claim.rationale: His rejection of Iraq’s annexation of Kuwait did not address every territorial claim acquired through conquest.

notes: Reviewed all active and candidate statements across economy, government, society, world affairs, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, political means and globalism. Follow-up on the uncertainty results included the UN speeches on apartheid, disarmament, international cooperation and aid, the 1992 agrarian reversal, statutory strike rules, Gulf War participation, the relationship between religion and the state, and the language of the 2007 constitutional changes. The security and economic answers use acts where the record settles the statement. The communications shutdown, proposed family succession, and limitations on political participation were examined separately. The shutdown record did not establish a personal order by Mubarak, and he did not transfer the presidency to his son. Follow-up also covered the signed Egypt–Sudan charter and the nationality amendment, which distinguish partial cross-border integration and dual nationality from universal open borders.
